title: Complete Vegan Protein Combinations: PDCAAS table + calculator | Hacé Cuentas
description: Check if your plant-based dish covers all 9 essential amino acids. Lentils+rice, hummus+pita, tofu+quinoa and more — PDCAAS score instant.
answerSnippet: Legumes (lentils, beans, chickpeas) are low in methionine; grains (rice, wheat) are low in lysine. Combining them during the day gives you a complete protein. Lentils + rice reach PDCAAS ≈ 0.95 — nearly equivalent to meat. Tofu and quinoa are already complete proteins on their own.
intro: The whole "you must combine proteins at every meal or you'll get sick" idea most people grew up with traces back to Frances Moore Lappé's *Diet for a Small Planet* (1971) — which Lappé herself **retracted** in the 1981 revised edition, writing she had overestimated the difficulty of getting enough protein on a plant-based diet. The science caught up in 1994 when Young and Pellett published their landmark paper in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* showing that the human liver maintains a free amino acid pool throughout the day — meaning a vegan eating a varied diet hits complete protein status without any mealtime choreography. That said, the **classic complementary combos** (rice and beans, hummus and pita, peanut butter on whole wheat) are still useful — especially for solo meals, athletes timing post-workout nutrition, or anyone eating one big plant-based plate as their main protein hit of the day. This calculator checks if your specific dish covers the bases and gives you the PDCAAS quality score along with the limiting amino acid.
keyTakeaway: **You don't need to combine at every meal** — daily variety is enough for healthy adults per the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics 2016 position paper. For solo plant-protein meals, pairing a grain (low lysine) with a legume (low methionine) gives a complete amino acid profile. PDCAAS scores: lentils + rice ≈ 0.95, tofu + quinoa ≈ 1.0, hummus + pita ≈ 0.90.
useCases: **Vegan athlete daily protein plan** — A 180-lb (82 kg) male cutting on a vegan diet targeting 198 g protein/day (2.4 g/kg) maps it out: 3 cups cooked lentils (54 g), 9 oz tempeh (63 g), 4 tbsp peanut butter (16 g), 6 oz seitan (50 g), and a scoop of pea-rice protein blend (25 g) = ~208 g, distributed across 4–5 meals with grain+legume pairings.

**Plant-based meal prep for the week** — Batch-cook Sunday for 5 weekday lunches: rice + black beans (Latin), lentil curry + brown basmati (South Asian), tofu stir-fry + quinoa (East Asian), chickpea pasta + marinara (Italian), and tempeh tacos on corn tortillas — each meal scoring complete on its own.

**Fitness vegan macro optimization** — A 145-lb female recreational lifter (1.6 g/kg = 105 g protein/day) wants to maximize leucine for muscle protein synthesis. The calculator helps her front-load 3 g leucine/meal: soy milk + oatmeal + 2 tbsp peanut butter (breakfast), edamame + brown rice bowl (lunch), seitan + quinoa (dinner).

**College student on a $40/week food budget** — Cheap staples (dry lentils $1.50/lb, brown rice $1.20/lb, peanut butter $3/jar, oats $0.10/cup) cover ~120 g protein/day. The calculator confirms which combos hit complete status.

example.title: Example: Lentils + Rice
steps: Lentils have Met+Cys as limiting amino acid (AAS ≈ 0.63); rice has lysine as limiting (AAS ≈ 0.56)
Combined, each provides what the other lacks — the blended profile raises both AAS scores
Combined PDCAAS ≈ 0.95 (out of 1.0) → nearly complete protein
example.result: Complete protein: Yes. Limiting amino acid: None. PDCAAS: 0.95

explanation:
## How Plant Protein Quality Works

Every plant food family has a predictable weak spot in its essential amino acid (EAA) profile. Knowing which family is short on what lets you pair them intelligently.

### Limiting amino acids by plant family

| Plant family | Examples | Limiting amino acid(s) | Pair with |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Grains** | Rice, wheat, oats, corn, barley | Lysine (low) | Legumes, soy |
| **Legumes** | Lentils, black beans, chickpeas, pinto, kidney | Methionine + cysteine | Grains, nuts, seeds |
| **Nuts & seeds** | Peanuts, almonds, sunflower seeds | Lysine (low) | Legumes, soy |
| **Soy** | Tofu, tempeh, edamame, soy milk | None — naturally complete | Stands alone |
| **Pseudocereals** | Quinoa, amaranth, buckwheat | None — complete | Stand alone |

### PDCAAS of the 5 classic combinations

| Combination | Complete? | Limiting amino acid | PDCAAS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lentils + Rice | Yes | None | ~0.95 |
| Hummus + Pita Bread | Yes | None | ~0.90 |
| Tofu + Quinoa | Excellent | None (both complete) | ~1.00 |
| Peanut Butter + Whole Wheat | Almost | Methionine traces | ~0.85 |
| Beans + Corn | Yes | None | ~0.90 |

### PDCAAS of individual plant foods (reference)

| Food | Limiting amino acid | PDCAAS alone | Best combination | PDCAAS combined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| White rice | Lysine | ~0.56 | + Lentils | ~0.95 |
| Lentils | Met + Cys | ~0.63 | + Rice | ~0.95 |
| Black beans | Met + Cys | ~0.60 | + Corn | ~0.85 |
| Corn | Lysine + Trp | ~0.42 | + Black beans | ~0.85 |
| Wheat (bread) | Lysine | ~0.47 | + Chickpeas | ~0.82 |
| Chickpeas | Met + Cys | ~0.71 | + Tahini | ~0.88 |
| Quinoa | None | ~0.92 | — (complete alone) | ~0.92 |
| Soy/Tofu | None | ~1.00 | — (complete alone) | ~1.00 |
| Pea protein | Met + Cys | ~0.82 | + Rice | ~0.96 |
| Sesame/Tahini | Lysine | ~0.50 | + Chickpeas | ~0.88 |

> Source: calculated from FAO/WHO and USDA FoodData Central composition data.

---

## DIAAS scores for common plant proteins

DIAAS (Digestible Indispensable Amino Acid Score, FAO 2013) is the newer, more accurate replacement for PDCAAS — it uses ileal (small-intestinal) digestibility and isn't truncated at 1.00. Per Mathai et al. (*Br J Nutr* 2017, PMID 28166859):

| Plant protein | DIAAS |
|---|---|
| Soy protein isolate | 0.99 |
| Pea protein concentrate | 0.93 |
| Chickpeas | 0.83 |
| Oats | 0.67 |
| Cooked rice | 0.59 |
| Wheat (whole grain) | 0.40 |
| Cooked corn | 0.36 |

---

## How the calculator works

The tool applies the PDCAAS method (FAO/WHO/UNU 1991):

```
PDCAAS = (mg limiting EAA per g protein in food)
          ÷ (mg same EAA per g protein in FAO/WHO reference)
          × True Fecal Digestibility (TFD)

Truncated at 1.00
```

### FAO/WHO/UNU EAA Reference Pattern (mg per g protein)

| Essential amino acid | Adults | Children 1–2 yr |
|---|---|---|
| Histidine | 15 | 26 |
| Isoleucine | 30 | 46 |
| Leucine | 59 | 93 |
| Lysine | 45 | 66 |
| Met + Cys | 22 | 42 |
| Phe + Tyr | 38 | 72 |
| Threonine | 23 | 43 |
| Tryptophan | 6 | 17 |
| Valine | 39 | 55 |

---

## Vegan athlete protein math (real example)

A 180-lb (82 kg) male in a cutting phase needs **2.4 g protein/kg** (ISSN 2017 position) = **~198 g/day**:

| Food | Serving | Protein |
|---|---|---|
| Cooked lentils | 3 cups | 54 g (18 g/cup) |
| Tempeh | 9 oz | 63 g (21 g per 3 oz) |
| Peanut butter | 4 tbsp | 16 g (8 g per 2 tbsp) |
| Seitan | 6 oz | 50 g (25 g per 3 oz) |
| Tofu (firm) | 6 oz | 20 g (10 g per 3 oz) |
| **Total** | | **~203 g** |

Doable on whole foods alone, no protein powder required.

---

## Common mistakes

1. **Believing the protein-combining myth.** Daily variety beats mealtime obsession.
2. **Skipping B12.** Non-negotiable supplement for vegans — 250–500 mcg cyanocobalamin/day.
3. **Ignoring vitamin C with iron-rich meals.** Triples non-heme iron absorption (Hallberg & Hulthén 1989).
4. **Using spinach as your calcium source.** Oxalates block absorption. Use bok choy, collards, or fortified plant milk.
5. **Underestimating leucine for muscle synthesis.** Aim for 3 g leucine/meal; soy, lentils + rice, and seitan + quinoa all clear it.

faq.q: Do I really need to combine proteins at every meal?
faq.a: No. The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics' 2016 position paper confirms that complementary plant proteins do **not** need to be eaten at the same meal — the liver maintains a free amino acid pool drawn from foods consumed throughout the day. Frances Moore Lappé, who popularized the protein-combining idea in *Diet for a Small Planet* (1971), retracted it herself in the 1981 edition. For healthy adults eating a varied vegan diet with adequate total protein, you'll hit complete amino acid status daily without mealtime choreography.

faq.q: What are the best naturally complete vegan proteins (no combining needed)?
faq.a: Five plant proteins are complete on their own: **soy** (tofu, tempeh, edamame, soy milk — DIAAS 0.99), **quinoa** (PDCAAS 0.92), **amaranth** (PDCAAS ~0.89), **buckwheat** (PDCAAS ~0.80), and **hemp seeds** (close to complete, mildly low lysine). Pea protein (DIAAS 0.93) is also effectively complete and is the base for most plant-based protein powders.

faq.q: Is B12 supplementation really necessary on a vegan diet?
faq.a: Yes. **B12 is non-negotiable on a vegan diet.** There is no reliable plant source — the B12 in spirulina, tempeh, and sea vegetables is a pseudo-B12 analog that the human body cannot use (Watanabe, *Exp Biol Med* 2014). The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, the British Dietetic Association, and the AAP all recommend B12 supplementation for vegans. Practical dose: **250–500 mcg cyanocobalamin daily** or 1,000 mcg twice a week.

faq.q: Is a peanut butter sandwich a complete protein?
faq.a: Not by itself. Peanut butter and whole-wheat bread **both** have lysine as their limiting amino acid, so combining them doesn't fix the gap — combined PDCAAS is around 0.50–0.55. The fix: add a lysine-rich food — a glass of soy milk, edamame, lentil soup, or hummus on the side. That completes the amino acid profile and also boosts total protein, calcium, and iron.

faq.q: Are vegans more prone to iron deficiency?
faq.a: Vegans have similar iron deficiency rates to omnivores in well-planned diets, even though plant (non-heme) iron has lower bioavailability (5–12%) than heme iron from meat (15–35%). The fix: (1) eat more iron-rich plants — lentils, tofu, tempeh, pumpkin seeds, fortified cereals; (2) **pair them with vitamin C** to triple absorption (Hallberg & Hulthén, *AJCN* 1989). Avoid coffee and tea within 1 hour of iron-rich meals.

Yes, with proper planning. Hevia-Larraín et al. (*Sports Medicine* 2021) ran a randomized controlled trial in resistance-trained men comparing vegan vs. omnivore diets matched for protein (1.6 g/kg) and found **identical gains in strength and muscle mass over 12 weeks**. Practical adjustments: aim for 1.8–2.2 g protein/kg (slightly higher than omnivores), hit 3 g leucine per meal, spread protein across 4–5 meals/day.

faq.q: How does plant protein quality compare to whey or eggs?
faq.a: Per the FAO's DIAAS scoring (Mathai et al., *Br J Nutr* 2017): whey isolate scores ~1.10, eggs ~1.13, soy isolate 0.99, pea protein 0.93, chickpeas 0.83, oats 0.67, wheat 0.40. Soy and pea are functionally equivalent to animal proteins for muscle synthesis at adequate doses. Lower-DIAAS plants aren't 'bad' — they just need pairing with a complementary plant (grain + legume) or higher total intake.

faq.q: Does eating soy mess with male hormones or cause gynecomastia?
faq.a: No. Messina's 2010 meta-analysis (*Fertility & Sterility*, 41 studies, 1,000+ men) found **no effect** of soy or isoflavone intake on testosterone, estrogen, free testosterone, or sperm quality at intakes up to 70 g soy protein/day — far more than any normal eater consumes. Three servings of soy daily (tofu, soy milk, edamame) is safe per AICR and ACS guidelines.

faq.q: What about omega-3s? Don't vegans need fish oil?
faq.a: Plant omega-3 (ALA) sources — flax (2.3 g ALA/tbsp ground), chia (2.5 g/oz), walnuts (2.5 g/oz) — convert to EPA/DHA at only 5–8% efficiency. For most healthy adults this is adequate with 1–2 servings/day. But during **pregnancy, lactation, infancy, and for older adults**, supplement with **algae oil (200–300 mg combined DHA + EPA/day)** — algae is what fish eat to get DHA in the first place.

faq.q: Can kids be raised vegan safely?
faq.a: Yes — with planning. The American Academy of Pediatrics (2023) and the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics state that well-planned vegan diets are appropriate at all life stages, including infancy. Critical points: (1) **B12 supplementation is mandatory**; (2) calorie density matters more for toddlers — include nut butters, avocado, olive oil; (3) hit higher pediatric EAA targets (lysine 66 mg/g, leucine 93 mg/g for ages 1–2); (4) iron, zinc, calcium, vitamin D, omega-3 (algae DHA), and iodine need active attention.

faq.q: How much more protein do vegans need compared to omnivores?
faq.a: The WHO base requirement is 0.83 g/kg/day for healthy adults. Because the average PDCAAS of plant proteins is lower than animal proteins, most nutrition authorities recommend vegans consume 10–20% more protein than omnivores — so approximately **1.0–1.1 g/kg/day** for sedentary vegans and **1.8–2.2 g/kg/day** for vegan athletes. On whole foods (lentils, tofu, tempeh, seitan), these targets are achievable without protein powder.
